summary.one_line: A tiny, promoter-controlled digital lender making very short, very expensive unsecured personal loans (effective APR 30%-86%), raising about Rs 32 crore of fresh equity only to fund more lending. Write-offs eat roughly a quarter of revenue, the promoter's holding company takes a management fee about 2.7x the company's own FY26 profit, and the DRHP lists several compliance lapses. There is no real moat. Avoid.
bull_points: All fresh issue, no offer for sale: the money goes into the company. Rs 32.00 crore is earmarked to augment the capital base for onward lending, and general corporate purposes are capped at the lower of 15% of gross proceeds or Rs 10 crore (S1, S7).

The loan book is growing fast. AUM rose from Rs 42.37 crore (FY24) to Rs 70.68 crore (FY26) and Rs 81.24 crore (31 Jul 2026), and fresh disbursements rose from Rs 174.68 crore in FY24 to Rs 306.25 crore in FY26 (S1, S7).

Restated revenue from operations grew 46.91% in FY26 to Rs 36.80 crore after a flat FY25, and PAT rose from Rs 0.45 crore (FY24) to Rs 1.97 crore (FY26). The four months to 31 Jul 2026 show PAT of Rs 3.01 crore on revenue of Rs 18.00 crore (S1, S7).
Capital is ample for now. CRAR was 28.57% at Mar-26 and 43.80% at 31 Jul 2026 after a Rs 15 crore equity infusion by the promoter company, against a 15% regulatory minimum (S1, S7, S12).
Early delinquency is improving on the company's own measure: accounts 90+ DPD at first EMI fell from 5.82% (FY23) to 2.44% (Q4 FY26) (S1).
bear_points: Credit losses are severe. FY26 irrecoverable debts written off were Rs 9.59 crore against revenue of Rs 36.80 crore and PAT of Rs 1.97 crore, and fresh NPA additions in FY26 (Rs 10.71 crore) equalled about 31% of the opening own loan book (S1).

Value leaks to the promoter. Capfront Technologies, 93.79% owned by CMD I.V.R. Gowrinath, charged a management fee of Rs 5.34 crore in FY26 (about 2.7x restated PAT) plus Rs 37.90 lakh rent. Rs 3.56 crore of 'claims receivable' was also owed by Capfront at Mar-26 (S1, S11).

The DRHP discloses compliance lapses: a board change made without the prior RBI approval it required, misreported NPA data in the FY24 DNBS02 return to RBI, NCD charges not registered and NCDs issued without an ISIN, untraceable RoC filings, and unpaid stamp duty on the business-transfer agreement with the parent (S1).

The lending is at the riskiest end of the market: unsecured loans of Rs 1,500 to Rs 2 lakh to first-time and lower-income borrowers at effective APRs of 30% to 86%. Only about 30% of FY26 revenue was interest, and the rest was platform fees, commissions and charges (S1).
Operating cash flow was negative at Rs -18.44 crore in FY26, and borrowings doubled to Rs 46.80 crore at an implied cost of about 19%, so the business depends on outside capital to grow (S1).
watch_points: Whether the parent's management fee, which fell to 8.21% of revenue in the four months to Jul-26 from 14.51% in FY26, stays low after listing. The stub-period margin jump partly reflects this promoter-controlled lever (S11).
Credit costs and write-offs in the first half-yearly results after listing, given loan growth of about 15% in four months to Rs 81.24 crore (S1, S7).
Any RBI action on the disclosed reporting and approval lapses, and the effect of the RBI Digital Lending Directions 2025 on default-loss guarantees and co-lending terms (S1, S23).
Final subscription by category and anchor names. As of the morning of 13 Oct 2026 no bids had been reported, and anchor allottee names were not found (S3, S14).

reasoning: The issue buys more of the same high-loss lending, not a moat. Rs 32 crore goes to the capital base to fund more unsecured personal loans (S1). The company's own industry chapter is generic macro filler (S1), and at about Rs 81 crore of AUM it holds roughly 0.05% of a Rs 1.54 lakh crore digital personal-loan market (S7, S21). The LoanFront app and underwriting are replicable features, not barriers.

Unit economics depend on extreme pricing that only just covers losses. Effective APRs run from 30% to 86% (S1), yet FY26 write-offs of Rs 9.59 crore plus provisions came to about Rs 11.5 crore, roughly 24% of average on-book loans (S1). FY26 PAT was only Rs 1.97 crore, a 5.36% margin (S1). A modest rise in defaults or an RBI pricing or conduct intervention would erase profit.

The minority shareholder sits behind the promoter's holding company. Capfront, 93.79% owned by the CMD, took a Rs 5.34 crore management fee in FY26, larger than PBT of Rs 3.15 crore (S1). It also owns the domains and carries the insurance, and it sub-leases the corporate office to the company (S1). The CMD draws no salary from the listed company (S1), so the CMD's economics flow through the parent rather than through the shares IPO investors buy.

The stub-period profit jump is not clean evidence of improvement. PAT of Rs 3.01 crore in four months coincided with the parent's fee falling to 8.21% of revenue from 14.51% (S11) and a Rs 15 crore pre-IPO equity infusion (S12). One independent reviewer flagged possible pre-IPO window dressing and suggested skipping the issue (S8).

Governance and compliance quality is weak for a regulated lender. The DRHP admits to a board change without the prior RBI approval it needed, misreported NPA data to RBI, unregistered NCD charges, missing RoC records and unpaid stamp duty (S1). The company lent Rs 55 lakh to its own MD in FY25 (S1), and the DRHP contradicts itself on the business-transfer price (Rs 2 crore vs Rs 1 crore) and on charge registration (S1).

subsections.title: What the company does and how it earns

blocks.text: Vaibhav Vyapaar Limited is a Kolkata-incorporated, RBI-registered non-deposit-taking NBFC (registration dated 18 Aug 2010) that lends unsecured personal loans through its 'LoanFront - Personal Loan App'. The work is run mostly from a Bengaluru corporate office (S1). Capfront Technologies Pvt Ltd bought 99.79% of the company in October 2019 and turned a dormant NBFC licence into the regulated lending entity for its LoanFront app (S1). The app, loan-management software, APIs and logo were then moved from Capfront into the NBFC in June 2022 on a slump-sale basis (S1, S13).

There are two products. Self-employed borrowers get Rs 1,500 to Rs 30,000 for 3 to 12 months, and salaried borrowers get Rs 10,000 to Rs 2,00,000 for 3 to 24 months. Both carry a stated interest rate of 17.50% to 33.94% a year plus processing fees of up to Rs 1,950 or Rs 2,500 and a one-time registration fee (S1). Customers are graded A to E, and the DRHP states that the effective APR ranges from 30% to 86% (S1). This is small-ticket, high-cost credit to borrowers with monthly incomes above Rs 25,000, including first-time borrowers (S1).

blocks.caption: Revenue from operations by type, restated (Rs lakh; share of total) (S1)
rows: Misc. (convenience, penalty, registration, credit-report fees etc.)

blocks.text: Only about 30% of FY26 revenue was loan interest. Platform fees, foreclosure charges, penalties and other borrower charges made up most of the rest (S1). On very short loans, upfront fees and charges largely explain the gap between the 17.5%-33.94% headline rate and the 30%-86% effective APR the DRHP discloses (S1). This revenue mix is the kind of practice RBI's digital-lending rules on all-in cost disclosure target (S23).

subsections.title: Operating model: direct lending, co-lending and services for other NBFCs

blocks.text: Loans are processed end to end in the app. The steps are OTP and email verification, PAN validation through NSDL APIs, pin-code serviceability, two OTP-verified references, digital or video KYC, penny-drop bank verification, a rule-based and ML credit model using bureau, device and behavioural data, Aadhaar e-sign, and disbursal to the borrower's bank account. Repayment is by eNACH, UPI or Bharat BillPay (S1). Collections escalate from automated calls before the due date to tele-calling, then agency-led recovery around 30-45 DPD and legal action around 45-60 DPD (S1).

Besides lending on its own book, the company co-originates loans with partner NBFCs and earns 'platform commission' for sourcing, KYC, collection and servicing done for other lenders under service agreements (S1). Named partners are Bhawana Capital (a service-provider agreement from April 2024) and Usha Financial Services (a co-lending agreement from 3 May 2025) (S1). Off-book AUM moved from a business-correspondent model in FY25 to co-lending in FY26 (S5). The company carries first-loss default guarantees on these arrangements, worth Rs 43.54 lakh at Mar-26 and about Rs 1.96 crore at Jul-26 according to an RHP-based summary (S1, S12).

Most of the technology stack is rented. Of 17 major software systems listed, only the loan-application front end is company-owned. Accounting, CRM, hosting, KYC, bureau pulls, penny-drop and dashboards all run on third-party licences (S1). The domains loanfront.in and vaibhav-vyapaar.com are registered to the parent and used under a no-objection certificate, and the company holds no insurance in its own name because cover sits with Capfront (S1). Headcount was 55 at Mar-26 (18 tech, 11 risk, 9 operations), and attrition was 34.00% in FY26 and 47.73% in FY25 (S1).

There is no factory, plant or capacity metric. The DRHP states that capacity and utilisation are 'not applicable' because the company is service-based (S1). Its scale measures are AUM, disbursements and app reach: 114 lakh downloads and Rs 1,500 crore of cumulative disbursements as of June 2026 (S1, S9). Combining about 24 lakh loans disbursed (S10) with Rs 1,500 crore cumulative gives an average ticket of roughly Rs 6,000, which is our own derivation.

blocks.caption: Loan book and disbursement scale (Rs lakh) (S1, S7)

blocks.text: Disbursements run at four to five times average AUM, which confirms how short the loans are: the book turns over several times a year (S1). There is no single-customer concentration, since the borrowers are lakhs of individuals. The real concentration is geographic and in the funding side. At Mar-26 the top five states held 77.09% of AUM: Tamil Nadu 22.71%, Karnataka 14.96%, Telangana 14.27%, Andhra Pradesh 13.74% and Maharashtra 11.41% (S1). Revenue shows the same southern skew (S1, S5). One RHP-based summary instead names Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal and Gujarat as concentrations at Jul-26 (S10, S17). We could not reconcile this with the DRHP's state tables and treat the DRHP as authoritative.

Repeat borrowers drive the business, contributing about 75%-82% of revenue and about 80% of AUM at Mar-26 (S1). That signals product stickiness, but it also means many customers keep rolling short, expensive loans. That is a regulatory and conduct sensitivity, not purely a strength.

The relevant market is digital-NBFC personal lending. FACE data based on CRIF High Mark records cover more than 110 digital NBFCs. By that data, outstanding digital personal loans stood at 5.6 crore accounts worth Rs 1.54 lakh crore at June 2026, up 28% year on year. Q1 FY27 sanctions were 3.4 crore loans worth Rs 64,656 crore, which is 70% of all personal-loan sanction volume but only 22% of value (S21). The average digital ticket was Rs 18,802, against Rs 70,025 at other NBFCs and Rs 4.52 lakh at banks. The industry's 90+ DPD ratio was 1.4% in June 2026 (S21).

The DRHP's own 'Industry Overview' is almost entirely generic IBEF and IMF macro material (GDP, UPI volumes, bank mergers). It gives no sizing of the digital personal-loan segment and no market-share claim for the company (S1). Management therefore offers no independent industry evidence for its positioning.

At Rs 81.24 crore AUM (S7), Vaibhav Vyapaar is about 0.05% of the Rs 1.54 lakh crore digital personal-loan book (S21), which is our calculation. Its average ticket of roughly Rs 6,000 (our derivation from S9 and S10) is about a third of the digital-NBFC average (S21), so it sits at the smallest, riskiest end of an already small-ticket segment.

The DRHP names Paisalo Digital, Apollo Finvest and Moneyview as listed peers (S4). An independent reviewer called these comparisons not truly comparable (S8). Beyond listed names, the field includes well-funded app lenders, bank and NBFC digital arms and fintech lending platforms. CB Insights' comparison set for Capfront includes Fibe, Navi, UGRO Capital, Vitto and others (S22). The DRHP itself describes the sector as 'highly competitive' and concedes that competitors 'may possess greater financial resources, larger distribution networks, stronger brand recognition or broader technological capabilities' (S1).

Funding is the competitive disadvantage that matters most. The company borrows from other NBFCs and through NCDs at 14% to 19.75% (S1, S12), and our calculation of its FY26 average cost of borrowing is about 19% (finance cost of Rs 6.64 crore on average borrowings of about Rs 34.7 crore) (S1). Bank-backed and larger NBFC competitors fund far more cheaply, so this lender can only compete at the top of the APR range.

No. The four 'competitive strengths' the DRHP lists are ground-level market understanding, a digital platform with in-house technology, an experienced management team and an underwriting framework (S1). These are generic claims every digital lender makes, with no market-share, import-substitution, licence-scarcity or technology claim behind them. The NBFC licence is not scarce, the app relies mostly on third-party KYC, bureau and hosting services (S1), and the brand domains belong to the parent (S1).

items: Data advantage: 86 lakh registered users and about 5 lakh customers (S10) give some repeat-borrower scoring history, which is a real but modest edge in a market of 5.6 crore digital loan accounts (S21).

Regulatory barrier: RBI rules, including 125% risk weights on unsecured consumer credit and the 2025 Digital Lending Directions, raise costs for everyone (S1, S23). They protect incumbents with cheap capital, not small lenders like this one.
Pricing power: none demonstrated. Rates at 30%-86% APR mainly compensate for credit losses (see Financials) rather than reflecting a franchise premium (S1).

blocks.text: We find no real moat. The business is a small regulated balance sheet attached to an app, competing on access for borrowers whom cheaper lenders decline (S1, S21).

blocks.caption: Restated statement of profit and loss (Rs lakh) (S1); 4M FY27 figures from RHP-based summaries (S7, S10)

blocks.text: Revenue was flat from FY24 to FY25 at about Rs 25 crore and then jumped 46.91% in FY26 as disbursements rose to Rs 306 crore (S1). FY25 PAT was helped by a Rs 3.42 crore reversal of NPA provisions and a deferred-tax credit (S1). The company paid no current tax in any of the three years (S1). The restatement cut audited PAT materially through deferred-tax adjustments: FY24 from Rs 131.61 lakh to Rs 45.48 lakh, and FY26 from Rs 236.63 lakh to Rs 197.10 lakh (S1).

The 'EBITDA margin' of 29.47% quoted on aggregator sites (S3) adds back finance cost, which is the main raw material for a lender, so it is not a meaningful measure. The meaningful line is PAT of Rs 1.97 crore on Rs 36.80 crore of revenue (S1).

subsections.title: Credit quality: the real cost line

blocks.caption: Asset-quality movement on own book (Rs lakh) (S1)

blocks.text: The headline GNPA ratio of 4.71% (and 4.56% at Jul-26 per S10) understates the losses. In FY26 Rs 10.71 crore of loans became NPA, about 31% of the Rs 34.14 crore own book at the start of the year, and about Rs 11.87 crore was written off (S1). Because loans are written off quickly, closing GNPA stays small. Our calculation puts FY26 credit costs (write-offs plus NPA and standard provisions, Rs 11.54 crore) at about 24% of average on-book loans and about 31% of revenue (S1). Provision coverage has also fallen: NNPA rose from 0.60% to 2.94% as the provision buffer shrank from Rs 2.24 crore to Rs 1.09 crore (S1).

The DRHP also admits that NPA recognition and provisioning were wrongly applied in the past. It says the FY24 DNBS02 return to RBI misreported asset-quality parameters, and that excess provisions were later reversed, 'resulting in reversals and fluctuations in reported income' (S1). Historical asset-quality figures therefore deserve extra scepticism.

subsections.title: Balance sheet, cash flow and leverage

blocks.caption: Balance sheet and cash flow (Rs lakh unless stated) (S1); Jul-26 from RHP-based summaries (S3, S7, S12)

blocks.text: Negative operating cash flow is normal for a growing lender, since loan disbursements are classified as operating outflows (S10). It still means growth has to be funded externally. FY26 financing inflows were Rs 23.60 crore, and borrowings more than doubled (S1). The jump in net worth to Rs 47.20 crore at Jul-26 came mainly from a Rs 15.00 crore equity subscription by Capfront in the stub period, not from earnings (S12, S14). Capitalised software and intangibles of Rs 6.89 crore are about 24% of FY26 net worth and are deducted from Tier I capital (S1).

Red flag: Capfront, the promoter's holding company, owed the lender Rs 3.56 crore of unexplained 'claims receivable' at Mar-26 (Rs 3.08 crore at Jul-26), about 12% of FY26 net worth (S1, S11). No settlement timetable is disclosed (S11). Meanwhile the same parent was paid Rs 5.34 crore in management fees (S1).

Does the trend support the growth story? AUM growth is real (S1), but profitability has not scaled with it. FY26 RoE was 6.99% (S1) on a book priced at 30%-86% APR, because losses, funding costs and the parent's fee absorb most of the yield. The better stub period coincides with a lower parent fee and fresh equity (S11, S12), not with a proven improvement in credit costs.

blocks.text: The task brief said the price band was not yet known. Several aggregators still show the old Rs 50-52 band (S6, S15, S24), but the issuer's 9 October corrigendum, reported by S7 and matched by the company press release (S9), fixes it at Rs 51-54. The DRHP was filed for 76,00,000 shares (S1), and the final RHP terms are 77,96,000 (S7, S9).

This is a pure fresh issue, so every rupee raised, net of expenses, goes to the company and no existing shareholder sells (S1, S7). The promoter's stake falls from about 99.99% to 72.34% through dilution, not a sale (S3).

blocks.text: The single real object is to raise Tier I capital so the company can borrow and lend more while staying above the 15% CRAR floor. The DRHP explicitly ties this to RBI's 125% risk weight on unsecured consumer loans (S1). The objects were not appraised by any bank or financial institution (S1, S7). Because the issue is below Rs 50 crore, no monitoring agency is required, so use of funds will be overseen only by the audit committee (S1).

The proceeds do not buy a new capability, plant or technology. They buy more balance sheet for the same high-loss lending, so the return on this capital depends entirely on credit costs staying contained. CRAR was already 43.80% at Jul-26 before the IPO money arrives (S7), which suggests the near-term need is about future growth headroom rather than an immediate capital shortfall.

items: Minimum promoter contribution (20% of post-issue capital) is locked in for 3 years (S1).
Promoter holding above the minimum is locked in on a phased basis under the ICDR (Amendment) Regulations, 2025: 50% for 2 years and 50% for 1 year (S1).
Pre-issue shares held by non-promoters (12 shares) are locked in for 1 year (S1).
Anchor investors: 50% for 30 days (to about 15 Nov 2026) and 50% for 90 days (to about 14 Jan 2027) (S1, S3).

blocks.text: Free-float supply pressure from insiders is limited, because the parent holds essentially all pre-IPO shares and these are locked for one to three years (S1). The first meaningful unlock is the anchor tranche at 30 and 90 days (S3). Since Capfront's stake is the CMD's stake, Capfront's own capital needs are worth watching once the first promoter tranche frees up after one year.

The promoters are Itha Venkata Raghava Gowrinath (47, B.Sc., M.Sc. in Computer Science), who is Chairman and Managing Director and holds 3,996 shares directly, and Capfront Technologies Pvt Ltd, which holds 2,03,82,415 shares (99.98%) (S1). Gowrinath founded Capfront in November 2018 and owns 93.79% of it, so economic control rests with one individual (S1). The DRHP describes 17+ years in 'technology-led operations, project execution and business management' but gives no lending track record (S1). A CB Insights profile lists the CMD's prior roles at KB NBFC, LeEco, Huawei and Samsung SDS (S22).

blocks.text: Most of the governance architecture, including the independent directors, CFO, CS and conversion to a public company, was put in place between November 2025 and June 2026 in preparation for the IPO (S1). The one independent director with deep sector experience (the ex-RBI supervisor) joined only weeks before the DRHP was filed (S1).

This RPT section is not routine. The management fee is the largest single cost after credit losses. At Rs 5.34 crore it was 14.51% of FY26 revenue and about 2.7 times FY26 restated PAT (S1, S11). The DRHP does not explain what services the fee buys or how it is priced (S11). Because the CMD takes no salary from the issuer but owns 93.79% of the fee recipient (S1), the CMD's incentives run through Capfront rather than through the listed shares. The fee fell to 8.21% of revenue in the four months to Jul-26 (S11), which flatters the pre-IPO stub profit and can be raised again at the parent's discretion.

items: The NBFC lent Rs 20 lakh (FY24) and Rs 55 lakh (FY25) unsecured to its own MD and earned interest on it. The loan was repaid by Mar-26 (S1).

The core platform was bought from the parent in 2022 with no disclosed independent valuation (S13). The DRHP gives the price as Rs 2 crore in one chapter and Rs 1 crore in another, and admits stamp duty on the agreement was not paid, relying on an indemnity from Capfront (S1).
Capfront guarantees at least Rs 14.34 crore, about 38%, of the company's borrowings (S12), which deepens the operational dependence on the parent.
Directors Gowrinath and Mallidi sit on the boards of both Capfront and the group company Neofront, which has lent to and bought 'other services' from the issuer (S1).
RBI: a board change that resulted in a change of management happened without the required prior RBI approval. The director later resigned, and no RBI action has been received (S1).
RBI: the FY24 DNBS02 return misreported NPA recognition and provisioning, and the company had applied incorrect NPA policies (S1, S10).

NCDs: CHG-9 charge filings were rejected by RoC and remain unregistered, and NCDs were issued without an ISIN, in non-demat form (S1). Note 33(f) of the restated accounts nonetheless states that no charges remain unregistered beyond the statutory period, which contradicts the risk factor (S1).
RoC: auditor-appointment forms for 2008-14 cannot be traced, and 13 forms were filed late (S1). Professional tax, PF and ESIC filings were delayed for short periods (S1).
Litigation: one tax proceeding against the company (Rs 2.3 lakh) and one against a director (Rs 0.76 lakh). No criminal or regulatory proceedings are pending (S1).

blocks.text: For an RBI-regulated lender, inaccurate regulatory returns, an unapproved management change and unregistered security on debt are more serious than the usual SME filing delays. Together with the internal inconsistencies in the DRHP, they point to weak control over regulatory obligations (S1).

items: Credit losses: unsecured loans to first-time, lower-income borrowers lead to write-offs of Rs 9-10 crore a year against PAT under Rs 2 crore (S1). A small rise in delinquency, for example from job losses or over-indebtedness across lending apps, would wipe out profit.

Funding cost and access: borrowings come from other NBFCs and NCDs at 14%-19.75%, with cash collateral of 5%-10% on several facilities, and about 38% of debt is backed by the parent's guarantee (S12). Losing a lender or the parent's guarantee capacity would constrain growth.
Geographic concentration: 77% of AUM is in five states, led by Tamil Nadu at 22.7% (S1). State-level action against lending apps or local shocks would hit the book disproportionately.
Platform dependence: critical KYC, bureau, payment and hosting functions run on third-party licences, and the domains belong to the parent (S1).

blocks.text: These are company-specific and quantified in the DRHP, unlike the generic interest-rate and macro risk factors that fill much of the section (S1).

items: Regulatory: high-APR, fee-heavy digital lending is a direct focus of the RBI Digital Lending Directions 2025, which require all-in cost disclosure, direct fund flows and caps on default-loss guarantees (S23). Any cap on effective pricing or fees would hit a model where fees and charges are about 70% of revenue (S1).
Past RBI lapses: the misreported DNBS02 return and the unapproved board change could still draw penalties or supervisory restrictions (S1, S10).
Promoter extraction: the management fee to Capfront (S1, S11) and unexplained claims receivable from the parent (S11) can move value away from minority holders.
Key-person and staffing: a 55-person company with 34%-48% annual attrition (S1) is thin for a regulated lender handling lakhs of borrower accounts.
SME liquidity: trading lots of 2,000 shares, a market maker holding only 3,90,000 shares, and 72% of shares held by the promoter mean limited exit liquidity (S3, S7).

blocks.text: Lock-in is not the main risk here. Promoter shares are locked for one to three years under the 2025 ICDR rules (S1), and the first sizeable unlock is the anchor tranche at 30 and 90 days after allotment (S3). The governance risks above are not time-limited.

Management has given direction but no numbers. The DRHP's strategy chapter lists four aims: upgrade the app and credit models, strengthen underwriting, add new loan products for salaried and self-employed borrowers, and expand co-lending partnerships with NBFCs (S1). It gives no AUM, disbursement, credit-cost or profitability targets (S1).

In the IPO-launch press release, CMD Gowrinath described the listing as a step in moving 'from an NBFC licence holder to a technology-led digital lending platform'. He cited 114 lakh downloads and Rs 1,500 crore of cumulative disbursements, and said proceeds would strengthen capital to support loan-book growth in line with RBI capital-adequacy norms, with priorities of disciplined underwriting, co-lending expansion and technology investment (S9). The lead manager's director cited smartphone penetration and demand for formal credit (S9), which is sell-side framing, not company guidance.
We found no investor call, interview or quantified guidance. Any outlook beyond 'more capital, more lending, more co-lending' would be our inference, not management's statement (S1, S9).

Mechanically, Rs 32 crore of new Tier I capital (S1) on top of Rs 47.20 crore of net worth (S3) could support a much larger book at leverage of about 1.6x (S1). Growth in AUM is therefore likely. Whether shareholders benefit depends on three things management has not addressed quantitatively: credit costs on a larger and probably less-seasoned book, whether the Capfront management fee returns to 14%-18% of revenue (S11), and whether regulation squeezes fee-based pricing (S23).

The digital personal-loan market is growing about 28% a year with improving industry delinquency (S21), so the tailwind is real. Industry 90+ DPD of 1.4% (S21) contrasts with this lender's annual NPA additions of about 31% of its opening book (S1), which shows it serves a riskier segment than the average digital NBFC.

This report was written on 13 Oct 2026, the opening day. As of 08:15 IST, one tracker showed 0x subscription in every category, with no bids reported yet (S14). Other trackers showed subscription data as pending (S3, S19). No category-wise QIB, NII or retail figures were available when this report was compiled, so no demand conclusion can be drawn.

The anchor book was scheduled for 12 Oct 2026 for up to 22,00,000 shares, worth about Rs 11.88 crore at Rs 54 (S3, S9). We could not find a published list of anchor allottees. Anchor lock-in is 50% for 30 days and 50% for 90 days (S1, S3).
Grey market premium (unofficial, unregulated): trackers reported a GMP of Rs 0 from 8 to 13 October 2026 (S4, S14, S16). This is not an investment signal and played no part in our verdict.

method: Primary source: the 324-page DRHP dated 01.07.2026. The NSE Emerge copy (S2) timed out on fetch, so the identical company-hosted copy (S1) was used and its pages were read directly. We covered risk factors, capital structure and lock-in, objects, business, history, management, promoters, group company, the full restated financial statements, notes on revenue, expenses, asset quality and capital adequacy, and the related-party note. The final RHP (NSE zip) could not be opened. RHP-only items were therefore cross-checked across at least two secondary sources: the revised Rs 51-54 price band and 77,96,000-share size (S3, S7, S9), the four-month FY27 stub financials (S3, S7, S10), Jul-26 AUM and CRAR (S7, S9, S10), and the stub management fee and Rs 15 crore Capfront equity infusion (S11, S12). The stub fee and the infusion each come from a single RHP-based analysis and are labelled as such. Aggregators conflict on the price band (older pages still show Rs 50-52), lot size, and Jul-26 AUM and net worth (some show Rs 812 crore and Rs 472 crore, which are scale typos). We used the issuer's corrigendum and the DRHP's tables. One source's state-concentration claim (UP, West Bengal, Gujarat) conflicts with the DRHP's state tables, which we follow. Credit-cost ratios, management-fee-to-PAT, average borrowing cost, average ticket size and market share are our own calculations from the cited figures. Industry sizing uses FACE/CRIF data via S21 because the DRHP's industry chapter is generic. Valuation is excluded by design, and no P/E, P/B or peer-multiple figures are used even where sources show them. Day-1 subscription was nil or pending when written, and anchor allottee names were not found. GMP is reported only as unofficial context.
